w: Frank Gehry's titanium curves went up beside the Nervion in 1997, and by the time King Juan Carlos I opened it with 250 contemporary works, critics and the public had already agreed on something rare - a genuine turning point in architecture. A 2010 survey still named it among the most important buildings since 1980.
s: Gehry's titanium curves that remade a city.
_facts: Museum of modern and contemporary art, inaugurated 18 October 1997 by King Juan Carlos I with 250 contemporary works
Designed by Frank Gehry, built alongside the Nervion River
Called a signal moment in architectural culture; named most frequently as one of the most important buildings completed since 1980 in a 2010 World Architecture Survey

w: Pilgrims on the Camino de Santiago passed through this church before Bilbao itself existed - the site may predate the city's 1300 founding. It only became a cathedral in 1955, but its neo-Gothic tower hides a genuine 15th-century cloister, plus stone carvings of local merchants worked into the buttresses.
s: A Camino waypoint older than Bilbao itself.
_facts: Dedicated to James the Great, a point of transit for Camino de Santiago pilgrims, UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2015
Origins probably predate the city's 1300 founding; built 14th-15th century as the main parish church
Elevated to cathedral status in 1955
Mixture of 15th-century Gothic cloister and Gothic Revival facade/tower; stone carvings of local merchants along the buttresses

w: Santiago Calatrava slung this tied-arch footbridge across the Nervion to link the Campo Volantin and Uribitarte riverbanks, its white steel arch becoming one of the signature images of Bilbao's riverside rebuild.
s: Calatrava's white steel arch over the Nervion.
_facts: Tied arch footbridge across the Nervion River, Basque for 'white bridge'
Designed by Santiago Calatrava
Links the Campo Volantin right bank and Uribitarte left bank

w: Tucked inside Dona Casilda Iturrizar park, this is the second-most-visited museum in the Basque Country after the Guggenheim - and arguably the deeper collection, running from El Greco and Goya through Gauguin and Sorolla to Francis Bacon and Richard Serra. One of the richest Spanish museums outside Madrid.
s: El Greco to Bacon, inside a city park.
_facts: Located entirely inside Dona Casilda Iturrizar park
Second largest and most visited museum in the Basque Country after the Guggenheim, one of the richest Spanish museums outside Madrid
Collection spans Middle Ages to contemporary, including El Greco, Cranach, Murillo, Goya, Van Dyck, Dore, Sorolla, Cassatt, Gauguin, Ensor, Bacon and Serra

w: Named for Juan Crisostomo de Arriaga - nicknamed 'the Spanish Mozart' - this riverside opera house has survived both fire and flood since Joaquin Rucoba built it in 1890, requiring two full reconstructions along the way. The same architect designed Bilbao's city hall just up the water.
s: Named for the 'Spanish Mozart,' rebuilt twice.
_facts: Opera house on the Nervion River, built in Neo-Baroque style by architect Joaquin Rucoba in 1890, who also built the city hall
Named after Juan Crisostomo de Arriaga, known as the 'Spanish Mozart'
Endured a fire and a flood, leading to two major reconstructions

w: Ricardo Bastida built this as a wine market in 1909; by the 1970s it sat abandoned, nearly demolished before the city settled on a culture centre instead. Philippe Starck reopened it in 2010 crammed with a cinema, library and pools, renamed for the mayor who saved it, Inaki Azkuna, five years on.
s: A 1909 wine market turned Starck-designed hub.
_facts: Originally a wine market (alhondiga) designed by Basque architect Ricardo Bastida, inaugurated 1909
Abandoned in the 1970s, several scrapped proposals including demolition, before 1994 decision to renovate into a sports/culture centre
Redesigned by Philippe Starck with Thibaut Mathieu, opened in stages in 2010 with a cinema, fitness centre, library, auditorium and shops
Renamed Azkuna Zentroa in 2015 in tribute to late mayor Inaki Azkuna

w: Biscay's patron saint, Our Lady of Begona, has her shrine in this basilica above the city - the province's principal seat of devotion, dedicated wholly to her image and cult, and one of Bilbao's oldest continuous acts of civic faith.
s: Shrine to Biscay's patron saint, Our Lady of Begona.
_facts: Basilica dedicated to the patroness saint of Biscay, the image of Our Lady of Begona

w: Bilbao's Biscay government once ran the province from the arcaded building on this neoclassical square before decamping in 1890 - the space now belongs to the Royal Academy of the Basque Language. Every Sunday the arches still host a flea market of old books, coins and birds, much as they've done for generations.
_facts: Monumental neoclassical square designed in 1821, inaugurated in 1851, enclosed by arcaded buildings accessed by arches called cuevas
Main building was seat of the Biscay government until a new palace was built in 1890; now site of Euskaltzaindia, the Royal Academy of the Basque Language
Every Sunday hosts a traditional flea market of old books, coins, stamps, birds and flowers

w: This Old Town church and the bridge beside it are so central to Bilbao's identity that both appear together on the city's coat of arms - a rare case of a parish church becoming municipal heraldry. The estuary still runs right past its walls.
s: The only church on Bilbao's own coat of arms.
_facts: Catholic church in the Old Town, dedicated to Anthony the Great
Featured, along with the San Anton Bridge, in the city's coat of arms
The estuary of Bilbao flows next to it

w: A funicular has hauled Bilbao's residents up this 300-metre hill since well before it became a tourist habit, depositing them at a summit park with restaurants and a hotel and the best panorama of the city and its estuary below. Lower and closer than its sister peak Pagasarri, it's the one locals actually use.
s: A funicular ride to the best view of Bilbao.
_facts: One of two small mountain ranges delimiting Bilbao (the other being Pagasarri), no more than 300 metres, closest to the city centre
Artxanda Funicular links downtown Bilbao with a recreational area at the top: a park, restaurants, hotel and sports complex
Offers panoramic views of the city to tourists

w: At 10,000 square metres of covered stalls, this is reputedly the largest covered market in all of Europe - fishmongers, butchers and greengrocers packed onto the Nervion's right bank right next to the old town, with a whole section reserved for local farmers selling direct.
_facts: Market square on the right bank of the Nervion River, next to Casco Viejo
Built area of 10,000 square metres, making it the biggest covered market in Europe
Stalls sell fresh produce, fish, meat and greengrocery, plus a section for local farmers' products

w: Merchants hauling goods from Biscay to Castile had no choice but this bridge - the only crossing over the estuary for centuries, first raised before 1318. Floods and wars knocked it down repeatedly since; the current structure dates only to 1937, but it still carries the city's coat of arms and Athletic Bilbao's crest.
s: The only crossing to Castile for centuries.
_facts: Oldest bridge in Bilbao, original opened before 1318, for centuries the only bridge crossing the river
Depicted on the city's coat of arms and Athletic Bilbao's crest
Rebuilt in 1880, damaged in the Carlist Wars, then reconstructed again in 1937 after demolition in the Spanish Civil War

w: You can start climbing this 673-metre peak straight from Bilbao's city streets, no car required - which is exactly what generations of weekend trekkers have done, following trails up through what its Basque name calls 'thick forest of beech' to a summit refuge overlooking the whole municipality.
s: A 673-metre peak you can climb from the street.
_facts: Basque name means 'thick forest of beech', part of the Basque Mountains
Main peak separates Bilbao municipality from Arrigorriaga and Alonsotegi, elevation 673 metres
Refuge near the summit is a popular destination for weekend trekkers climbing directly from the city streets

w: Whoever designed this Flemish-style mansion apparently refused to repeat a single window - every set on the facade is different, a deliberate echo of the Renaissance palazzos of Antwerp and Bruges. It now houses the Spanish central government's delegation to Biscay.
s: No two windows alike, Flemish style in Bilbao.
_facts: Building in Flemish style around Eliptica Square, built early 20th century, style resembles Renaissance palaces of Antwerp and Bruges
None of the sets of windows on the facade is the same as any other
Now accommodates the representation of the Government of Spain in the province of Biscay

w: Sailors coming home up the Nervion once first glimpsed the Basilica of Begona's tower at this bend - and, so the story goes, began praying their thanks to the Virgin then and there. The spot's landmark, the 1970s Salve Bridge, now runs so close to the Guggenheim it appears to merge into the museum.
s: Where sailors first glimpsed home, and prayed.
_facts: Name comes from sailors returning from sea first seeing the tower of the Basilica of Begona at this point on the river Nervion
Folklore holds they would start praying to the Virgin of Begona, patron saint of the region, thanking her for protection
Main landmark today is La Salve Bridge, built in the 1970s, which gained popularity when the Guggenheim Museum was built right under it, merging its structure into the museum's
